equity.level_reason: Rates are reported by urbanization level (rurality) and sex, with the highest rates in large central metropolitan areas described, but no disparity is framed or quantified.

level_alternative.reason: Urbanization could be read as geography rather than social position, leaving only sex, which keeps the level at 0.

ev.q: Counties were classified using the 2013 National Center for Health Statistics Urban-Rural Classification Scheme for Counties.
Rates were higher for males than for females at each urbanization level.

equity.equity_measurement: County urbanization uses the six-level 2013 NCHS Urban-Rural Classification Scheme; there is no referent group and no computed contrast.

ev.q: Rates were the highest for males (4.4) and females (1.8) in large central metropolitan areas.

notes: The CIs are shown as error bars, but no claim is stated to rest on them, so no CI-based test is recorded. The male–female contrast within each urbanization level is read as stratified, although the values are only set side by side.
view_issues: The prepass cue 'percentage' is a false hit; the article reports only rates. The source line says 2018–2021, but the data shown are for 2021.
